title: Truth and deception
note: Disingenuous (falsely sincere) is nearly the opposite of ingenuous (innocently frank). A canard is a false story, an apocryphal tale is widely told but of doubtful truth, and a Potemkin village is a showy front built to hide a poor reality, named for stories of fake villages shown to Catherine the Great.

items.a: lying; not telling the truth
items.ex: The mendacious ad claimed the cereal cured insomnia.

items.a: truthfulness; conformity to fact
items.ex: Reporters questioned the veracity of the senator's war stories.

items.a: deceitfulness; double-dealing
items.ex: His duplicity came out when both rivals compared the promises he had made them.

items.a: to hide one's true feelings or motives
items.ex: She dissembled her disappointment behind a bright smile.

items.a: to speak evasively to avoid the truth
items.ex: When asked where the money went, the treasurer began to prevaricate.

items.a: the use of trickery to deceive
items.ex: Accounting chicanery hid the losses for three years.

items.a: deceit used to achieve a goal
items.ex: By a clever subterfuge, the prisoners made the guards count wrong.

items.a: a trick meant to fool someone
items.ex: The "gas leak" was a ruse to get the family out of the house.

items.a: a false or unfounded report
d: a story told for moral teaching
items.ex: The old canard that we use only ten percent of our brains refuses to die.

items.a: widely told but of doubtful truth
items.ex: The tale of young Washington and the cherry tree is apocryphal.

items.a: false or fake; not genuine
items.ex: The "ancient" coin turned out to be a spurious copy minted in 1990.

items.a: insincere while pretending to be frank or naive
items.ex: It was disingenuous of him to act surprised by a plan he had drafted.

items.a: innocent and frank; unsuspecting
items.ex: The ingenuous tourist handed his wallet to a stranger who asked to see it.

items.a: treacherous; betraying trust
items.ex: The perfidious ally switched sides on the eve of battle.

items.a: a person who falsely claims skill or knowledge
items.ex: The charlatan sold "magnetic water" at three county fairs.

items.a: a swindler, especially a showy seller of fake remedies
d: a person who mocks for fun
items.ex: The mountebank on the wagon promised his tonic would grow hair on glass.

items.a: an impressive front hiding a poor reality
d: a community run by its residents
items.ex: The model school was a Potemkin village, polished for the inspectors' visit.

items.a: a thing that is not what it is claimed to be
items.ex: The election was a sham; the results were printed before the polls opened.

items.a: to pretend to feel or have
items.ex: The opossum feigned death until the dog lost interest.

items.a: to deceive or trick
items.ex: Investors were duped by a website full of stock photos.

items.a: too ready to believe things
items.ex: Only a credulous reader would trust a headline ending in three exclamation points.

items.a: a false statement meant to damage a reputation
d: a widely told but doubtful tale
items.ex: The rival spread a calumny that the chef reused leftovers.

items.a: the appearance of being true or real
items.ex: Period-accurate slang gave the novel its verisimilitude.

items.a: genuine; made in good faith
items.ex: After years of street shows, she became a bona fide star.

items.a: to expose the falseness of
items.ex: The museum's exhibit debunks a dozen myths about Vikings.

items.a: to trick or deceive
items.ex: The forger hoodwinked experts at two auction houses.

items.a: sleight of hand; skillful trickery
items.ex: Through budgetary legerdemain, the deficit vanished from the summary page.

items.a: a false reason given to hide the real one
d: a summary at the start of a book
items.ex: He visited on the pretext of returning a book, but he wanted to see the house.

items.a: clever trickery, or a clever device
items.ex: The magician's best artifice was making the audience look the wrong way.

items.a: plain and straightforward; not embellished
items.ex: The coach gave the team an unvarnished account of how badly they had played.

read.title: The Talking Horse
text: In the early 1900s a retired Berlin schoolteacher named Wilhelm von Osten announced that his horse, Hans, could do arithmetic. Asked what three plus two made, Hans tapped his hoof five times. Crowds gathered, and newspapers called him Clever Hans.

Was it chicanery? Many assumed von Osten was a charlatan running a ruse, but he was not trying to dupe anyone. He sincerely believed in the horse, and Hans answered correctly even when strangers asked the questions. A commission of experts found no sign of a deliberate trick.

The psychologist Oskar Pfungst finally debunked the claim in 1907, without accusing anyone of duplicity. He showed that Hans failed when the questioner did not know the answer, or when the horse could not see the questioner. The horse was reading tiny, unconscious changes in posture and face: people tensed as the count approached the right number and relaxed when it arrived.

The case is a lesson for credulous audiences and confident experts alike. The appearance of intelligence had real verisimilitude, and nobody involved was mendacious. Yet the conclusion was spurious. Scientists still design experiments so that no one present can give away the answer, a safeguard born from a horse in a Berlin courtyard.

o: the psychologist who exposed the horse
was secretly signaled by von Osten on purpose
